newsitem.title: INDONESIA: East Timor's "Foreign Minister" gets Nobel award.
newsitem.headline: East Timor's "Foreign Minister" gets Nobel award.

text.p: The award of the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize to East Timor's Catholic Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo and resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta recognised two men who dedicated themselves in different ways to the troubled territory.

Ramos-Horta, 48, is the driving force behind and spokesman for Fretilin, the main East Timorese group which resisted Jakarta's rule following the Indonesian invasion and annexation of the former Portuguese colony 20 years ago.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee said it had made the award to the two men "for their work toward a just and peaceful solution to the conflict in East Timor."

"I receive the news with pleasure and with sadness," Ramos-Horta said in a radio interview monitored in Lisbon. He said Fretilin's military leader Xanana Gusmao, who is serving a 20-year prison sentence in Jakarta, should have had the prize.
Ramos-Horta fled East Timor three days before the Indonesian invasion in December 1975. He has now settled in Sydney, Australia, but campaigns around the world for independence for East Timor.
Even before the Portuguese departure, he had advocated East Timorese independence and in 1970 was exiled to Mozambique for two years by the Lisbon authorities for his activities.
Two of his brothers and a sister died when Indonesian troops invaded the predominantly Roman Catholic territory 2,000 km (1,200 miles) east of Jakarta.
He was then acting as secretary for foreign affairs and information for Fretilin, the Revolutionary Front for the Liberation of East Timor, the main group seeking Timorese independence.
The United Nations has refused to recognise Indonesia's annexation of the territory and still regards Portugal as the administering power.
